Material and methods
Study participants
Our study was based on a nested case-control study that included 196 incident T2D cases and 196 non-T2D controls from the CRISPS cohort
[26]
,
[27]
(
Fig. 1
,
Supplementary Table 1
), who had been investigated in our previous lipidomic analysis for incident T2D
[28]
. The CRISPS cohort is a prospective, population-based longitudinal cohort designed to investigate the development of cardiovascular risk factors, including T2D, in Hong Kong from 1995 to 2008. Details of the CRISPS cohort have been described previously
[27]
. Briefly, 2895 unrelated subjects of Chinese ancestry were selected randomly by their telephone numbers from the Hong Kong population, and invited to undergo a comprehensive assessment in 1995–1996. Participants were then invited to participate in the prospective follow-up assessments for the development of major cardiovascular risk factors in 2000–2004 (CRISPS 2), 2005–2008 (CRISPS 3), 2010–2012 (CRISPS 4) and 2016–2018 (CRISPS 5).
Fig. 1
Profound perturbation of plasma metabolome preceding T2D onset. (A) A schematic summary of the workflow for this study. (B) The proportions of annotated metabolites in our study. (C) Partial least-squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) based on 578 annotated metabolic features. (D) Metabolic networks showing pathways undergoing significant changes preceding T2D onset. Yellow nodes, pathway names; red nodes, metabolites enriched in incident T2D; blue nodes, metabolites enriched in the non-T2D group; grey nodes, metabolites not detected in our samples. Metabolites in the same pathway were annotated with the same shape with corresponding pathway names. Each edge represented the metabolic process based on KEGG database. Solid edges represented one-step reactions, and dashed edges indicated reactions with two or more steps. CE, cholesterol ester; DG, diglyceride; LPA, lysophosphatidic acid; LPC, lysophosphatidylcholine; LPE, lysophosphatidylethanolamine; LPI, lysophosphatidylinositol; PC, phosphatidylcholine; PE, phosphatidylethanolamine; PI, phosphatidylinositol; SM, sphingomyelin. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
All participants in the study had their blood taken after a 10-hour overnight fast at each visit. Details regarding anthropometric measurements and biochemical parameter measurement methods were previously described
[27]
. Except for those participants who are taking antidiabetic medications, a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was performed. The definition of T2D was based on the World Health Organization's 1998 diagnostic criteria, which considers a fasting glucose (FG) level of ≥ 7.0 mmol/L or a 2-h plasma glucose (2hG) level of ≥ 11.1 mmol/L, or the use of antidiabetic medications, as indicative of T2D
[29]
. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters
[30]
. Homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was calculated as fasting insulin (µU/L) × FG (mmol/L)/22.5, while homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function (HOMA-β) was calculated as [20 × fasting insulin (µU/mL)]/[FG (mmol/L) − 3.5]
[31]
. Triacylglycerol to high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol ratio (TG/HDL ratio) was calculated as TG (mg/dL) divided by HDL(mg/dL). High-density lipoprotein-cholesterol to low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol ratio (HDL/LDL ratio) was calculated as HDL (mg/dL) divided by LDL(mg/dL). Triglyceride-glucose index (TyG index) was calculated as ln[triglycerides (mg/dL) × FG (mg/dL)/2]
[32]
. Quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI) was calculated as 1/{log[fasting insulin (μU/mL)] + log[FG (mg/dL)]}
[31]
.
Clinical outcome
The eligible baseline population included those who were free from T2D at CRISPS-2 (baseline of this study) and with available plasma samples for the metabolomics analysis. Incident T2D cases were identified as those having T2D at CRISPS-3, CRISPS-4, or CRISPS-5 visits. Non-T2D controls were individuals who remained free of T2D at the end of the study (CRISPS-5). To minimize the possible effects of lipid-lowering drugs on lipid metabolism, individuals who were taking these medications at baseline were excluded from the eligible baseline population. For this nested case-control study, each of the 196 incident T2D cases was matched by age and sex with a non-T2D control by the propensity score matching method. The median follow-up period was 15.57 years (interquartile range [IQR] 9.98–16.97).
Ethics statement
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority, Hong Kong West Cluster (IRB reference no. UW 10-038). Informed consent was obtained from all subjects.
Metabolic profiling
Sample preparation.
A mixture of chilled methanol/acetonitrile/water (2:2:1, v/v/v, 400 μL) containing a series of internal standards (D
4
-serotonin, D
5
-tryptophan, D
4
-dopamine, 2-chloroadenosine, D
3
-methionine, 4-chlorokynurenine, 4-chloro-phenylalanine,
13
C
6
-arginine) was added to 30 μL plasma to precipitated protein followed by vortex and centrifugation. Two aliquots (180 μL) were taken and lyophilized. The residues were redissolved in 65 μL of acetonitrile/water (1:9, v/v) and 65 μL of acetonitrile/water (4:1, v/v) respectively for reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) and hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) analysis. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by combining an equal volume of each plasma sample and then processed as described above.
UHPLC-MS/MS analysis.
Metabolic profiling of plasma samples was similar to previous methods with modification
[33]
,
[34]
. Briefly, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)-based global metabolomics data were collected by using ultra high performance liquid chromatography coupled with a Q Exactive Focus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). RPLC and HILIC analysis were combined to expand metabolite coverage. RPLC analysis was performed on an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm, Waters, USA) with an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 guard column (5 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm, Waters, USA) equipped on an Ultimate 3000 rapid-separation liquid chromatography system for separation at 30 ℃. In positive ion mode, the mobile phases were water (A) and acetonitrile (B), both with 0.1% formic acid. In negative ion mode, the mobile phases consisted of water with 0.05 mM ammonium fluoride (A) and acetonitrile (B). The LC gradient program was as follows: 0 min, 2% B; 1 min, 2% B; 19 min, 100% B; 21 min, 100% B; 21.1 min, 2% B and 25 min, 2% B. The flow rate was 0.3 mL/min. The injection volume was 5 μL. HILIC analysis was conducted on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 1.7 μm, Waters, USA) coupled with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide guard column (5 × 2.1 mm, 1.7 μm, Waters, USA). The chromatographic and mass spectrographic parameters were the same as those described previously
[34]
. Full scan mode followed by ddms2 scan based on the data-dependent acquisition and parallel reaction monitoring mode was applied to obtain MS/MS spectra for metabolite identification.
Data analysis.
MS data were processed according to a previously reported method
[35]
. Metabolites were annotated by comparing the exact mass, MS/MS pattern and isotope pattern of metabolites in QC samples with those of commercial standards and public databases [METLIN (
https://www.metlin.scripps.edu
), MoNA (
https://mona.fiehnlab.ucdavis.edu/
), HMDB (
https://www.hmdb.ca/
), mzCloud (
https://www.mzcloud.org
), Massbank (
https://massbank.eu/MassBank/
)].
Targeted metabolomics
Targeted analysis of 14 metabolites selected by Boruta
[36]
was conducted on a Vanquish™ UHPLC System coupled to TSQ Altis™ Triple Quadrupole Mass Spectrometer (QqQ MS, Thermo Scientific, USA). Chromatography parameters were the same as our methods of untargeted metabolomics. The data were acquired by using the selected reaction monitoring mode. The data process was performed by TraceFinder Software (version 4.1, Thermo Scientific, USA). Compounds were quantified using the calibration curves of corresponding standards. The linearity was constructed by graphing the peak area ratio of each standard to the internal standard against corresponding concentrations of standard with the application of a 1/X2 weighting factor. Intraassay coefficients of variance showed values less than 20.0% for each metabolite, based on plasma quality control samples placed every 20 samples.
Statistical analysis
Comparison of incident T2D group and non-T2D group was done using the Mann-Whitney
U
test. Alongside principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least-squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) to view the relationship of metabolite expression between groups, the analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) test was performed to evaluate the dissimilarity of metabolic covariates using the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix. Marginal effects (adjusted R
2
) were calculated based on distance-based redundancy analysis using the vegan R package. Before evaluating the marginal effect of each clinical parameter on the metabolic variations, all parameters were examined by the removal of collinearities according to the variation inflation factor with a cutoff of 10, producing 22 nonlinear variables (age, sex, BMI, 2hG, waist-hip ratio, cholesterol, dyslipidemia, TyG index, HOMA-IR, HOMA-β, ALT, AST, HDL/LDL ratio, treatment with beta-blockers, treatment with angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, treatment with thiazides, gamma-glutamyl transferase, physical exercise, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, coronary heart disease, and stroke history). The marginal effect (adjusted R
2
) was evaluated after excluding contributions from all other variables (permutations = 9999). Next, associations between individual metabolites and clinical indices were assessed using boosted additive generalised linear models after adjustment for age, sex and BMI based on the “Maaslin2” R package. Bi-directional mediation analysis was done using the “mediation” R package.
Boruta, a random forest-based classification algorithm
[36]
, was adopted to capture the important variables in the metabolic dataset that are related to future T2D outcomes based on their importance compared to shadow features, their consistency across iterations, and statistical tests to validate their significance. To assess the independent association with T2D risk, metabolites were transformed by natural logarithm and included in conditional logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, TyG index, waist-hip ratio, 2hG, insulin and HDL/LDL ratio. These covariates in conditional logistic regression models were independently associated with metabolic compositional variations based on the results of distance-based redundancy analysis. To avoid colinearity, the more relevant variable of a pair of highly correlated variables was included, and repetitive clinical parameters were excluded. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was performed for multiple tests. The parsimonious final model, which included age, BMI, TyG index and 2hG, was built by Akaike information criterion in a stepwise algorithm. We investigated the predictive ability of the T2D risk model by calculating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). To investigate the prediction increment of new metabolic markers from pre-defined risk categories, the net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination index (IDI) and decision curve analyses were performed. P value less than 0.05 and FDR less than 0.1 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
Type 2 diabetes (T2D) has become a major global health problem
[1]
. Over the past decades, the prevalence of diabetes in China has grown remarkably. Among Chinese adults, the prevalence of diabetes soared from 5.5% in 2001 to 12.4% in 2018
[2]
,
[3]
. The high prevalence of diabetes imposes a considerable economic burden on societies
[3]
. The discovery of predictive biomarkers for early clinical screening is of great importance for the prevention of diabetes.
A prediction algorithm is a computational tool to assess an individual's risk of developing a particular disease, and plays a crucial role in the medical field by enabling early detection, personalized interventions and public health planning
[4]
. Conventionally, a T2D prediction algorithm may incorporate multiple factors such as demographic information, clinical measurements, lifestyle factors and biomarkers to generate a predictive score or probability of T2D onset within a certain timeframe
[5]
,
[6]
. In the past decade, increasingly complex information regarding an individual’s phenotypes, such as metabolic profiles, has denoted an area of intense research interest beyond conventional demographic information
[7]
. The plasma metabolome contains a large number of biomarkers that participate in disease pathways
[7]
. Characterization of the metabolites can offer novel insights into the pathogenesis of T2D and improve the prediction of the disease. Indeed, recent metabolic investigations in longitudinal epidemiological studies have identified various biomarkers for the prediction of diabetes risk
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
,
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
. Findings from previous observational studies suggest that several increased amino acids (such as valine, leucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine and glutamine) have strong correlations with insulin resistance and can predict disease progression and intervention outcomes
[15]
,
[16]
,
[17]
,
[18]
. Altered bile acid profiles, characterized by changes in specific bile acid species or ratios, have been observed in individuals with diabetes or those at high risk of developing the disease
[19]
. However, the prior work in the Asian population was indeed limited by a relatively short follow-up duration and only a small number of metabolites were interrogated
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
,
[20]
.
The relative contributions of insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction in the pathogenesis of T2D among Asian populations remain controversial. A previous prospective cohort study of Chinese subjects found that insulin resistance was significantly associated with a higher risk of diabetes compared with β-cell dysfunction, and this association pattern was more pronounced in the adult obese population
[21]
. By contrast, other studies have revealed that β-cell dysfunction plays a bigger part in T2D development than insulin resistance in Asians compared to Caucasians and Africans
[22]
,
[23]
,
[24]
. Furthermore, another multi-ethnic cohort study in Singapore reported that Asians who have prediabetes had worsened impairments in pancreatic insulin secretion and attenuated defects in peripheral insulin sensitivity
[25]
. There have been appeals to understand and identify the factors that make people susceptible to (or protected from) insulin resistance or β-cell dysfunction
[7]
.
Metabolomic profiles based on prospective, population-based longitudinal cohort studies may highlight the metabolic changes that cause insulin resistance or β-cell dysfunction accounting for future T2D development. In this study, our major objective was to identify metabolic biomarkers that could contribute to the development of T2D by performing a mass spectrometry-based metabolomics analysis in plasma samples from participants of the Hong Kong Cardiovascular Risk Factor Prevalence Study (CRISPS) cohort
[26]
,
[27]
, and examine whether the impact of these metabolites on T2D is mediated through insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction.

Results
Profound perturbation of metabolome preceding T2D onset
To comprehensively profile the plasma metabolome, we analyzed samples from 196 incident T2D cases and 196 age- and sex-matched non-T2D controls (
Supplementary Table 1
) for polar and non-polar metabolomes (
Fig. 1
A). A total of 578 metabolic features were annotated across the samples following the quality control procedures (
Fig. 1
B,
Supplementary Table 2
). Of these, 539 features were annotated with a metabolomics standards initiative (MSI) level 1 or 2 identification
[37]
. The samples were distributed based on the first two principal components according to their groups in the score plot of the PLS-DA. (
Fig. 1
C). There was a significant dissimilarity in the metabolic profile between incident T2D and non-T2D groups (
p
< 0.001). In addition, 140 features were significantly altered in the incident T2D group compared to the non-T2D group at baseline (
p
< 0.05,
Supplementary Table 2
). The perturbed metabolites were primarily lipids (accounting for 66%) but also included nucleotides, amino acids and peptides. The altered lipids were mostly glycerophospholipids, such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), lysophosphatidylcholines (LPC), lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE), lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI), phosphatidylcholines (PC) and phosphatidylinositol (PI). LPAs, LPCs, LPEs and PC plasmalogens decreased before T2D onset. By contrast, LPIs, diacyl PCs and diacyl PIs increased before T2D onset alongside diglycerides (DGs). Dysregulation of bile acids, acylcarnitines and sterol lipids was also observed.
Metabolite pathway altered before T2D onset
Altered metabolites of the same pathways tended to cluster together in the correlation matrix (
Supplementary Fig. 1
). The metabolic network showcased the pathways that changed preceding the onset of T2D (
Fig. 1
D). Most of the perturbed plasma metabolites were annotated within 13 KEGG pathways. Among the altered pathways, ether lipid metabolism and sphingolipid metabolism showed decreased activity prior to T2D onset (
Fig. 1
D). Conversely, amino acids and related pathways were enriched in the incident T2D group, such as phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism; tryptophan metabolism; alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism; valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation; arginine and proline metabolism. In addition, there were activated purine metabolism and caffeine metabolism in the incident T2D group. We also observed dysregulated glycerophospholipid metabolism and bile acid metabolism involving the gut microbiome.
Patterns in metabolite change according to insulin resistance
Next, we investigated the independent associations between metabolic shifts and clinical parameters. The results showed that the TyG index explained most of the observed metabolic shifts (
Fig. 2
A), indicating that the variations were more strongly associated with insulin resistance (TyG index) rather than β-cell dysfunction (HOMA-β). The TyG index was shown to contribute to a larger extent to the metabolic variations compared to HOMA-IR. The overall metabolic shifts were in parallel with the TyG index as shown in the PCA analysis (
Fig. 2
B-C). In contrast, a similar pattern in HOMA-IR was not observed (
Supplementary Fig. 2
A).
Fig. 2
Associations of metabolites with clinical risk factors. (A) Clinical indices exhibited an independent association with metabolic variations after excluding contributions from all other variables. (B) Principal component analysis (PCA) based on the metabolic features of plasma samples. The first two principal components were shown. Each sample’s color corresponded to its TyG index. (C) Scatterplot and regression line of TyG index against PCA dimension 1. The 95% confidence intervals for the slope of the line were shown by the shaded areas. (D) Heatmap of the associations between metabolites and clinical indices (
q
< 0.01 in boosted additive generalised linear models after adjusted for age, sex and BMI). Red and blue colors indicated positive and negative correlations respectively. 2hG, 2-h plasma glucose; BMI, body mass index; Coeff, coefficient; FG, fasting glucose; HOMA-IR, homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance; HOMA-β, homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function; HDL/LDL ratio, high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol to low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol ratio; QUICKI, quantitative insulin sensitivity check index; TG/HDL ratio, triacylglycerol to high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol ratio; TyG index, triglyceride-glucose index. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
Then we investigated the correlations between individual metabolite and clinical indices. As expected, the Venn plot revealed that more metabolites showed correlations with the indicator of insulin resistance, TyG index (
Supplementary Fig. 2
B). One hundred eighty-eight annotated metabolites were significantly correlated with the TyG index. The TyG-associated metabolites were shown to be overlapped with features that were associated with the TG/HDL ratio (
Fig. 2
D). Also, amino acid derivatives, DGs, glycerophospholipids and bile acids, were shown to be strongly associated with insulin resistance (TyG index and HOMA-IR) and insulin sensitivity (QUICKI) (

A putative causal role of the metabolites in future T2D mediated by insulin resistance
Subsequently, we systematically evaluated the putative causal relationships between metabolites, clinical risk factors and future T2D. A total of 457 mediation links were established for the contribution of metabolites to incident T2D mediated by clinical risk factors (

Among them, 20.6% of mediation linkages were in control of insulin resistance (TyG index and HOMA-IR) and 10.3% were through insulin sensitivity (QUICKI). In particular, TyG index mediated 22%, 48% and 40% of the effect of DG(18:2/22:6), acetyl-tryptophan and dimethylguanidino valeric acid on T2D, respectively (

Metabolic signatures predicting T2D identified by machine learning
We next built a machine learning classifier to discriminate individuals with incident T2D from those without the development of T2D using the metabolomes. Fourteen metabolic features were selected by the Boruta analysis (
Supplementary Fig. 6
).
To identify independent metabolic predictors for T2D, the 14 selected metabolic features were accurately quantified by the targeted LC-MS/MS method (
Supplementary Fig. 7
) and included one by one into the conditional logistic regression model adjusted for age, sex, BMI, TyG index, waist-hip ratio, 2hG, insulin and HDL/LDL ratio (see methods). Of these 14 metabolites, acetyl-tryptophan, kynurenine, γ-glutamyl-phenylalanine, DG(18:2/22:6), DG(38:7), LPI(18:2) showed independent positive associations with T2D risk (
q
< 0.1), whereas LPC(P-16:0), LPC(P-18:1), LPC(P-20:0), LPE(P-20:0) negatively correlated with T2D risk (
Fig. 5
A).

To establish risk stratification for the early identification of high-risk individuals and T2D prevention, we investigated the predictive value of these 10 metabolites which showed independent associations with the onset of T2D. The best clinical model predictive of incident T2D comprised of age, BMI, TyG index and 2hG. We found that clinical risk factors showed moderate prediction ability with a mean cross-validation AUROC of 0.846 (age + BMI + TyG + 2hG) (
Fig. 5
B). Adding the 10 metabolites significantly enhanced the model performance, reaching an AUROC of 0.894 (age + BMI + TyG + 2hG + Metabolites) (
p
< 0.001 by the Delong test). Inclusion of these 10 metabolites into the traditional clinical model led to a significant improvement with an NRI of 55.1% (95% CI 15.0–75.9%) and IDI of 11.2% (95% CI 0.08–14.4%), suggesting the contribution of these metabolites to risk stratification models for incident T2D. In decision curve analysis, which accounts for both calibration and discrimination performance in measuring net benefit, the result indicated that the combination of conventional clinical predictors and the metabolomic features equalled or outperformed established predictors (
Supplementary Fig. 8
).
Discussion
Untargeted metabolomics enables a broad range of metabolites to be characterized. This rich source of information could facilitate the elucidation of the underlying pathological progression of the disease. In this long-term prospective, population-based longitudinal cohort study, we observed profound perturbations of metabolomes and functional pathways preceding the development of T2D, allowing for an in-depth understanding of metabolic changes in the host. We also identified several T2D-associated metabolites that were revealed in previous studies, such as enriched amino acids and derivatives, downregulated sphingolipids, dysregulated bile acids and glycerophospholipids
[10]
,
[38]
,
[39]
,
[40]
. The altered glycerophospholipids, including plasmalogens of LPCs, LPEs, PCs and PEs, indicated the presence of lipid dysfunction, ROS-induced oxidation and peroxisomal disorder in incident T2D individuals
[41]
. It has been found that sphingomyelins (SMs) were inversely associated with T2D risk in the PREDIMED cohort
[42]
, which was confirmed in the current study. Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA; valine, leucine and isoleucine) and the byproducts of their catabolism, such as propionyl-carnitine, affect the development of insulin resistance and pancreatic β cell impairment in diabetes
[15]
,
[16]
. Elevated phenylalanine can impair insulin signaling and inhibit glucose uptake through modification of insulin receptor β
[17]
. In addition, several less well-studied amino acid derivatives were found to be associated with T2D or its related disorders. For example, dimethylguanidino valeric acid was defined as an independent biomarker of T2D, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and cardiometabolic dysfunction, and was associated with attenuated improvements in insulin sensitivity after exercise
[43]
,
[44]
; N-lactoyl-phenylalanine was found to be a circulating marker of NADH-reductive stress correlating with the mitochondrial disorder
[45]
. The orchestrated elevation of conjugated bile aids (glycocholic acid, taurodeoxycholic acid, taurohyocholic acid) before T2D onset as observed in the current study was consistent with previous studies
[10]
,
[19]
.
Our finding revealed the association between the metabolomes and insulin resistance (TyG index), which was independent of confounders such as physical exercise, age, sex, BMI and treatment. Previous research has indicated ongoing debate regarding whether metabolome impacts insulin resistance or β-cell dysfunction responsible for diabetes development in the Chinese population
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
,
[24]
. In the current study, we demonstrated that insulin resistance rather than β-cell dysfunction was strongly associated with metabolic shifts before overt T2D. Importantly, TyG index has been found to be strongly associated with muscle insulin resistance, whereas HOMA-IR showed more correlation with hepatic insulin resistance
[32]
,
[46]
,
[47]
. Compared to HOMA-IR, more circulating metabolites were linked to the TyG index. This observation suggests that metabolic perturbation before T2D development showed more correlations with muscle insulin resistance than hepatic insulin resistance in Chinese. However, we did not directly measure insulin resistance and β-cell function using the glucose clamp technique, and the results should be interpreted cautiously given the limitations of surrogate indices.
In line with our findings, recent longitudinal studies also revealed a close relationship between the metabolome and insulin resistance, such as amino acid derivatives, DGs, glycerophospholipids, acylcarnitines and bile acids
[13]
,
[40]
. Of note, these metabolites have been demonstrated to affect insulin signaling or insulin resistance
[15]
,
[17]
,
[19]
,
[28]
,
[48]
,
[49]
,
[50]
. In addition, the established mediation linkages indicated that the impact of metabolites on T2D risk could be mediated by insulin resistance. However, as these findings are mostly generated from observational data, further functional experiments focusing on specific metabolites are needed to confirm the causality.
Risk stratification is a critical component in T2D prevention. We developed and validated a prediction model for future T2D development. The combination of metabolomic information and conventional clinical risk factors in the prediction model showed good predictive performance and classification accuracy. Among those predictive metabolites, increased DG(18:2/22:6) and decreased LPC(P-16:0) showed correlations with elevated T2D risk, as we previously reported
[28]
. Moreover, our study was the first to demonstrate the inverse associations of LPC(P-18:1), LPC(P-20:0) and LPE(P-20:0) with incident T2D, whereas DG(38:7) was positively correlated with T2D risk. The underlying pathogenesis for the role of LPC-plasmalogens is thought to potentiate insulin secretion in mouse islets
[28]
. Additionally, peroxisome-derived plasmalogens are present in mitochondria whose dysfunction provokes insulin resistance
[51]
,
[52]
. Inhibition of plasmalogen synthesis impairs mitochondrial function which could be rescued by dietary supplementation of plasmalogen precursors
[51]
. It is reported that plasma membrane
sn
-1,2-DGs induces PKC∊-mediated hepatic insulin resistance
[49]
. On top of lipids, 3 amino acid derivatives (acetyl-tryptophan, kynurenine, γ-glutamyl-phenylalanine) were positively associated with T2D risk, in agreement with findings from previous studies
[13]
,
[40]
,
[53]
. In the PREDIMED trial, kynurenine predicted increased HOMA-IR
[54]
. Notably, adipocyte-derived kynurenine stimulates insulin resistance and obesity by activating the AhR/STAT3/IL-6 signaling
[48]
. The evidence was consistent with our findings that metabolites (DGs, kynurenine, plasmalogens) contribute to T2D risk as mediated by insulin resistance.
This study has a few limitations. The sample size of the nested case-control study within a long-term prospective cohort is relatively small. Additionally, our 10 metabolites-based prediction model for T2D has not been validated in an independent longitudinal cohort.
Conclusions
The current study identified a panel of metabolic biomarkers that were able to predict T2D onset, which may be potentially used for the precision management of T2D. Furthermore, our findings support the notion that the metabolic shifts driven by insulin resistance rather than β-cell dysfunction in turn cause T2D.
